aiSummary: Speckled trout are the dominant target across Choctawhatchee Bay right now, with good numbers scattered bay-wide and guides reporting consistent action despite recent wind; a bull redfish over 40 inches was also recently landed out of the Santa Rosa Beach area, signaling that big reds are actively cruising. Today's full moon is driving spring tides with a strong tidal push — high tide came early this morning around 5:22 AM and the drop runs all day toward a late-afternoon low near 4:38 PM, so that falling tide will be the primary moving-water window. Plan your morning around the bite and be off the water or tucked into protected bayous by early afternoon, as a 25% storm chance kicks in after 1 PM with a heat index pushing 111°F.

bridge.aiNote: The 331 Bridge spans the narrow neck of Choctawhatchee Bay, creating a current funnel that pushes bait through on both tides and concentrates speckled trout, redfish, sheepshead, and black drum around its pilings year-round. The lee-side pilings are the prime ambush zone on incoming tides, as fish stack up to intercept baitfish swept through the funnel. Keep in mind this is one of the most exposed spots on the bay — open water and chop make it the first location to become unfishable when wind builds.
bridge.todaysCall: With winds light out of the west at 0–10 mph this morning, the bridge should be fishable early, but plan to be there at first light and work efficiently — the falling tide running all day toward the 4:38 PM low means current will be moving through the pilings for most of the morning. Focus on the downcurrent lee-side pilings where trout and reds will be sitting in the ambush zone as bait gets swept through; the full moon's spring tide amplifies that flow, so expect a stronger-than-average current push. Water clarity is slightly stained, which actually favors natural-colored soft plastics and noisy top-waters to help fish locate your bait. With storms possible after 1 PM and this being the most exposed spot on the dashboard, commit to a hard out by noon — this is not the place to be when weather builds.

alaqua.aiNote: Alaqua Bayou offers protected water with a strong year-round redfish population, plus trout and flounder at the mouth where oyster bars mark the prime holding structure. Tree cover keeps interior water a few degrees cooler than the open bay and provides genuine shelter from wind and weather. The upper creek transitions toward brackish conditions and can hold bass alongside small redfish.
alaqua.todaysCall: Alaqua is a smart choice today — the tree cover and protected layout give you a reasonable weather buffer if afternoon storms fire earlier than the 1 PM window, and the cooler interior temps are welcome with the water sitting at 86°F bay-wide. Work the oyster bars at the creek mouth during the falling tide this morning; the full moon's spring tide will pull water out steadily all day, concentrating bait and fish along those bar edges. Slightly stained water calls for darker or chartreuse soft plastics and weedless gold spoons to maximize visibility for reds cruising the shallows. The bay-wide redfish bite has been active — this is a logical spot to encounter those fish given the consistent population here.

basin.aiNote: Basin Bayou sees lighter pressure than many nearby spots, which tends to mean less-educated fish and a more relaxed bite. Interior grass flats are classic sight-fishing territory for redfish in under two feet of water, and pompano occasionally show at the mouth on moving tides in late spring and early summer. It offers less weather protection than LaGrange when conditions deteriorate.
basin.todaysCall: The falling tide running toward the late-afternoon low is your best window on the interior grass flats today — moving water in skinny water will push reds into predictable ambush positions along flat edges and potholes. With the full moon driving stronger tidal flow, expect fish to move actively; get on the flats early before the sun angle gets high and the heat index climbs toward 111°F. Slightly stained clarity works against pure sight-fishing here, so cover water with weedless soft plastics or a gold spoon rather than waiting to spot-cast. Because Basin is less protected than LaGrange, keep a close eye on western skies after noon and be ready to run — storms are possible after 1 PM and you'll want an escape plan.

lagrange.aiNote: LaGrange Bayou is consistently rated the top trout producer among the bayous on this side of the bay, with legendary oyster bars at the mouth and interior grass flats that hold redfish year-round. Deep holes inside hold black drum and sheepshead, making it one of the most species-diverse inshore spots on the dashboard. It's also the most protected water on this side of the bay, making it the default go-to when weather builds.
lagrange.todaysCall: LaGrange is the top pick today for both the trout bite and storm insurance — if afternoon weather forces you off open water, you can keep fishing here longer than almost anywhere else on the dashboard. Work the mouth oyster bars hard during the falling tide this morning, as the full moon's spring tide will push a strong current through that structure and stack trout and reds in textbook feeding positions. The bay-wide speckled trout bite has been excellent, and LaGrange's reputation as the top trout producer makes this the highest-percentage play; soft plastics on a light jig head or a suspending twitch bait over the bars should be the first call in slightly stained water. If the morning trout bite slows, drop a crab or cut bait into the interior deep holes for black drum and sheepshead while you wait out the heat.

fourmile.aiNote: Four Mile Creek is a short tidal creek running between Shipyard Marina and the bay, making it one of the most convenient and most protected fisheries on the dashboard. Tidal flow pushes baitfish up the creek on incoming tides, concentrating redfish and trout in the bends and along grass edges, while the creek mouth is a prime flounder zone. The upper section transitions toward brackish water and can hold bass alongside small reds.
fourmile.todaysCall: Four Mile Creek is the easiest bail-out option if weather threatens — it's close to the ramp, short, and protected, which matters on a day with a 25% storm chance after 1 PM. Today's tide is falling all day toward the late-afternoon low, so focus on the lower creek bends and grass edges where fish will compress as water drains out; the full moon spring tide means that drain happens with authority. Work the creek mouth carefully for flounder, especially in the deeper slots at the channel edge — slightly stained water calls for bright or scented soft plastics to trigger a reaction. This spot rewards anglers who want a quick, low-commitment morning session with a fast return to the ramp if lightning pops up.

hogtown.aiNote: Hogtown Bayou is a signature Santa Rosa Beach guide destination and one of the most productive trout flats on Choctawhatchee Bay, with speckled trout consistently stacking on grass in two to four feet of water during summer mornings. Spanish mackerel show at the mouth on moving tides, adding an exciting bonus species. It sees regular guide and recreational pressure but produces reliably — summer mornings are the peak window.
hogtown.todaysCall: Hogtown is a high-percentage trout play today — summer morning conditions with a full-moon falling tide are exactly the setup that concentrates fish on the grass flats in two to four feet, and the bay-wide trout bite has been strong. Be on the water at first light and work the flats before sun angle and heat drive fish deeper; with a heat index forecasted near 111°F, the bite window will compress quickly as the morning progresses. Slightly stained water means fish are slightly less spooky but also harder to see, so cover water efficiently with a soft plastic on a light jig head or a popping cork rig. Factor in run time from the 331 Bridge — this is farther than the Freeport-side bayous, so leave early enough to fish the best part of the tide and still be heading in before the post-1 PM storm window opens.

rocky.aiNote: Rocky Bayou sits inside Fred Gannon Rocky Bayou State Park near Niceville, offering a scenic, significantly less-pressured alternative to the bayous closer to the 331 Bridge. Freshwater influence from Rocky Creek makes flounder fishing excellent, and the glass-calm state park coves are well-suited to sight-fishing for redfish. Mangrove snapper hold near dock and pier pilings, adding a bonus species rarely found at other dashboard locations.
rocky.todaysCall: Rocky Bayou's light pressure and state park setting make it a worthwhile trip on days when the more accessible bayous feel crowded, and the calm coves are ideal for working the falling tide across shallow reds today. Target the cove edges and grass lines during the morning falling tide, and pick apart any dock or pier pilings you encounter for mangrove snapper — a small jig or live shrimp tight to the structure is the play. Slightly stained water won't hurt the flounder bite; work the deeper channel edges and holes near the Rocky Creek influence with a bottom-bouncing jig or live mud minnow. Rocky Bayou is the furthest location from Shipyard Marina — plan your run time carefully and commit to leaving no later than noon given the post-1 PM storm chance.

mack.aiNote: Mack Bayou sits on the barrier-island (30-A) side of Choctawhatchee Bay near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park, well west of the 331 Bridge — a long-run destination rather than a quick local trip. It shares the same protected-bayou character as Alaqua and LaGrange, with marsh grass, oyster bars, interior holes, and lighter pressure simply due to its distance from the main ramps. Hewett Bayou and Buck Bayou sit immediately to the east and are realistically fishable in the same trip.
mack.todaysCall: Mack Bayou rewards anglers willing to make the run with less-pressured fish and classic protected-bayou habitat; the falling tide today will pull water off the marsh grass and oyster bars steadily through the morning, positioning reds and trout in predictable feeding lanes. Work the oyster bar edges at the mouth first on the dropping tide, then move interior as water pulls back and concentrates fish. With the run time factored in, you'll want to leave the ramp at or before first light to capitalize on the best tidal window before heat and storm risk build — the 25% storm chance after 1 PM is a real logistical constraint this far from the ramp. Consider pairing this with a quick swing through Hewett Bayou on the same trip to maximize the run.

hewett.aiNote: Hewett Bayou sits immediately east of Mack Bayou on the barrier-island (30-A) side of Choctawhatchee Bay, near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park, and shares the same protected character — oyster bars and marsh grass at the mouth with deeper interior holes further in. Light pressure due to distance from the main ramps is its defining advantage. It pairs naturally with Mack and Buck Bayou and is best approached as part of a combined western bay run.
hewett.todaysCall: Hewett fishes best as a tag-along with Mack Bayou — running both on the same trip makes the long haul worthwhile and lets you compare fish activity across two lightly pressured bayous. The falling tide this morning will move water through the oyster bar structure at the mouth; work those edges for trout and reds before pushing into the interior holes. Slightly stained water and the full moon's stronger tidal pull give you good conditions for targeting fish actively feeding on the moving tide rather than sitting tight. Same hard rule as Mack: be heading back by noon at the latest given the run distance and the post-1 PM storm window.

buck.aiNote: Buck Bayou is the smallest and least-documented of the three neighboring bayous on the barrier-island (30-A) side of Choctawhatchee Bay near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park. Its habitat likely mirrors Mack and Hewett — marsh grass, some oyster structure, and a modest interior — but there's less basis to speak with confidence about specific fish-holding features. It's best treated as a bonus stop on a Mack and Hewett Bayou trip rather than a standalone destination.
buck.todaysCall: Buck Bayou is worth a look if you're already running Mack and Hewett — it's right there and the light pressure alone makes it worth a few casts on the off chance fish are holding. Probe the mouth structure on the falling tide with the same approach you'd use next door: weedless soft plastic or gold spoon along any oyster edges you can find, and a slow-rolled jig in any deeper interior pockets. Temper expectations compared to its neighbors — less is known about this spot's specific structure and fish-holding features. Keep it brief and treat it as a bonus, not the anchor of the trip.
